claim: Escalated and inappropriate levels of aggressive behavior referred to as pathological in psychiatry can lead to violent outcomes with detrimental impact on health and society.
source: Escalated and inappropriate levels of aggressive behavior referred to as pathological in psychiatry can lead to violent outcomes with detrimental impact on health and society.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established knowledge about pathological aggression and its societal impacts.

claim: Early life stressful experiences might increase the risk of developing pathological aggressive behavior in adulthood.
source: Early life stressful experiences might increase the risk of developing pathological aggressive behavior in adulthood, though molecular mechanisms remain elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a premise in the abstract, supported by the study's rationale.

claim: Peripubertal stress (PPS) exposed Balb/c adult male mice exhibit escalated aggression.
source: We provide prefrontal cortex and hypothalamus specific transcriptome profiles of peripubertal stress (PPS) exposed Balb/c adult male mice exhibiting escalated aggression
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 1.

claim: Adult female mice are resilient to PPS-induced aberrant behavioral responses.
source: adult female mice resilient to such aberrant behavioral responses
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data showing females did not exhibit escalated aggression.

claim: Transthyretin (TTR) is a key regulator of PPS induced escalated aggressive behavior in males.
source: We identify transthyretin (TTR), a well known thyroid hormone transporter, as a key regulator of PPS induced escalated aggressive behavior in males.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptome data, gene knockdown experiments, and behavioral assays.

claim: Brain-region-specific long-term changes in Ttr gene expression were evident in PPS induced escalated aggressive male mice.
source: Brain-region-specific long-term changes in Ttr gene expression and thyroid hormone (TH) availability were evident in PPS induced escalated aggressive male mice, circulating TH being unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data showing differential Ttr expression in hypothalamus and PFC across different time points.

claim: Thyroid hormone (TH) availability was altered in brain regions of PPS induced escalated aggressive male mice.
source: Brain-region-specific long-term changes in Ttr gene expression and thyroid hormone (TH) availability were evident in PPS induced escalated aggressive male mice, circulating TH being unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements of T4 and T3 in hypothalamus and PFC.

claim: Circulating thyroid hormone levels were unaltered in PPS induced escalated aggressive male mice.
source: Brain-region-specific long-term changes in Ttr gene expression and thyroid hormone (TH) availability were evident in PPS induced escalated aggressive male mice, circulating TH being unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by serum T4 and T3 measurements showing no significant differences between control and PPS groups.

claim: Ttr promoter methylation marks were altered in hypothalamus and prefrontal cortex of PPS-exposed males.
source: Ttr promoter methylation marks were also altered being hypermethylated in hypothalamus and hypomethylated in prefrontal cortex corroborating with its expression pattern.
evidence: This is supported by MeDIP-qPCR data showing differential methylation patterns in the two brain regions.

claim: Ttr promoter was hypermethylated in hypothalamus of PPS-exposed males.
source: Ttr promoter methylation marks were also altered being hypermethylated in hypothalamus and hypomethylated in prefrontal cortex corroborating with its expression pattern.
evidence: This is supported by MeDIP-qPCR data in Figure 7.

claim: Ttr promoter was hypomethylated in prefrontal cortex of PPS-exposed males.
source: Ttr promoter methylation marks were also altered being hypermethylated in hypothalamus and hypomethylated in prefrontal cortex corroborating with its expression pattern.
evidence: This is supported by MeDIP-qPCR data in Figure 7.

claim: Ttr knockdown in hypothalamus resulted in escalated aggressive behavior in males without PPS.
source: Further, Ttr knockdown in hypothalamus resulted in escalated aggressive behavior in males without PPS and also reduced TH levels and expression of TH-responsive genes (Nrgn, Trh, and Hr).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from stereotaxic injection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ttr knockdown in hypothalamus reduced TH levels.
source: Further, Ttr knockdown in hypothalamus resulted in escalated aggressive behavior in males without PPS and also reduced TH levels and expression of TH-responsive genes (Nrgn, Trh, and Hr).
evidence: This is supported by T3 measurements in hypothalamus after Ttr esiRNA injection shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ttr knockdown in hypothalamus reduced expression of TH-responsive genes Nrgn, Trh, and Hr.
source: Further, Ttr knockdown in hypothalamus resulted in escalated aggressive behavior in males without PPS and also reduced TH levels and expression of TH-responsive genes (Nrgn, Trh, and Hr).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Escalated aggressive behavior was evident in next generation F1 male progenies of PPS-exposed males.
source: Escalated aggressive behavior along with reduced Ttr gene expression and TH levels in hypothalamus was also evident in next generation F1 male progenies.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from F1 males shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Reduced Ttr gene expression in hypothalamus was evident in F1 male progenies of PPS-exposed males.
source: Escalated aggressive behavior along with reduced Ttr gene expression and TH levels in hypothalamus was also evident in next generation F1 male progenies.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data from F1 males shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Reduced TH levels in hypothalamus were evident in F1 male progenies of PPS-exposed males.
source: Escalated aggressive behavior along with reduced Ttr gene expression and TH levels in hypothalamus was also evident in next generation F1 male progenies.
evidence: This is supported by T3 measurements in F1 males shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Animal aggression is considered escalated and pathological if it displays short attack latency, prolonged attack duration, attacks targeted on inappropriate partners, and body parts prone to serious injury; attacks not signaled by threats; or ignorance of signals of opponents.
source: Animal aggression is considered escalated and pathological if it displays short attack latency, prolonged attack duration, attacks targeted on inappropriate partners, and body parts prone to serious injury; attacks not signaled by threats; or ignorance of signals of opponents (Bacq et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a definition cited from the literature (Bacq et al., 2020).

claim: Animal models of escalated aggression can largely explain abnormal aggressive behavior in humans.
source: In general, animal models of escalated aggression can largely explain abnormal aggressive behavior in humans (Miczek et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to Miczek et al., 2015.

claim: Mounting epidemiological evidences link early life stressful experiences with deteriorating mental health.
source: Mounting epidemiological evidences link early life stressful experiences with deteriorating mental health (Nelson and Trainor, 2007; Duke et al., 2010; Haller et al., 2014; Hunt et al., 2019; Mitchell and Aamodt, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Stress exposures around puberty including childhood and adolescence confers susceptibility to aggressive behavioral disorders.
source: In particular, stress exposures around puberty including childhood and adolescence including fear, maltreatment, physical and sexual abuse confers susceptibility to aggressive behavioral disorders (Veenema, 2009; Tzanoulinou and Sandi, 2017; Bounoua et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Márquez et al., 2013 developed a novel animal model which showed the effect of peripubertal fearful exposures on male pathological aggression at adulthood in Wistar Han rats.
source: Márquez et al., 2013 developed a novel animal model which showed the effect of peripubertal fearful exposures on male pathological aggression at adulthood in Wistar Han rats.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study that developed the animal model used in this work.

claim: Hypothalamus is a key brain region for expression of aggressive behavior.
source: Hypothalamus is a key brain region for expression of aggressive behavior and neural circuit-specific manipulation experiments revealed that ventromedial hypothalamus is the crucial for inter-male aggression (Lin et al., 2011; Falkner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on neural circuits of aggression.

claim: Ventromedial hypothalamus is crucial for inter-male aggression.
source: Hypothalamus is a key brain region for expression of aggressive behavior and neural circuit-specific manipulation experiments revealed that ventromedial hypothalamus is the crucial for inter-male aggression (Lin et al., 2011; Falkner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neural circuit manipulation studies.

claim: PFC plays a regulatory role in inhibition of threat provoked aggressive behavior.
source: While Hypo is considered as the trigger center for aggression, PFC plays opposite regulatory role being involved in inhibition of threat provoked aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about PFC function in aggression regulation.

claim: Direct neuronal projections from PFC to Hypo have been suggested to control both type and amplitude of aggressive behavior.
source: More importantly, direct neuronal projections from PFC to Hypo have been suggested to control both type and amplitude of aggressive behavior (Choy et al., 2018; Biro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on PFC-hypothalamus connectivity.

claim: In adult control Balb/c mice, 95% were non-aggressive while 5% showed normal offensive aggression but not escalated.
source: We observed that in adult control (Ctrl-RI; N=60) Balb/c mice, 95% (N=57) were non-aggressive (Nagg) while 5% (N=3) showed normal offensive aggression (Lagg) but not escalated.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral screening data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Amongst PPS exposed adult male mice, 78.33% showed escalated aggression with pathological signs.
source: Amongst PPS exposed adult male mice (PPS-RI; N=60), 78.33% (N=47) showed escalated aggression with pathological signs characterized by prolonged fighting with short attack latency, attack on females and anesthetized intruder in all the sessions tested.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral screening data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: 32 out of 60 PPS-exposed males (53.33%) showed extremes of behavioral changes with greater than 80% observation time spent in attack and very short attack latency of less than one minute.
source: Amongst these 47 mice, 32 (53.33%) showed extremes of behavioral changeswith greater than 80% observation time spent in attack, very short attack latency of less than one minute in all the sessions (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—source data 1) and those which attacked both females and anaesthetized intruder.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral screening data presented in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Females did not show escalated aggression.
source: As reported earlier (Falkner et al., 2016) females did not show escalated aggression.
evidence: This is an observation from the study, also supported by a citation to Falkner et al., 2016.

claim: In hypothalamus of SEagg males, 49 genes were differentially expressed with 28 down-regulated, 20 up-regulated and 1 expressed only in SEagg males.
source: In Hypo, 49 genes were differentially expressed amongst which 28 were down-regulated, 20 were up-regulated and 1 was expressed in SEagg males but not in control males.
evidence: This is a summary of transcriptome analysis results presented in Figure 1D and E.

claim: PFC of SEagg males showed 87 DEGs with 57 downregulated, 28 upregulated and 2 only expressed in SEagg males.
source: PFC of SEagg males showed 87 DEGs amongst which 57 were downregulated, 28 were upregulated and 2 were only expressed in SEagg males but not control males (Figure 1D and E and, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of transcriptome analysis results presented in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Cell type analysis of top ranking DEGs showed highest number of neuron and microglia enriched genes followed by equivalent number of endothelial, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes enriched genes in Hypo.
source: Cell type analysis (https://www.brainrnaseq.org/) of top ranking DEGs showed highest number of neuron and microglia enriched genes followed by equivalent number of endothelial, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes enriched genes in Hypo.
evidence: This is based on cell type enrichment analysis using a publicly available database, with results shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2–8.

claim: PFC showed highest number of neuron and astrocytes enriched genes followed by equivalent number of microglia, endothelial and oligodendrocytes enriched genes.
source: PFC showed highest number of neuron and astrocytes enriched genes followed by equivalent number of microglia, endothelial and oligodendrocytes enriched genes (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–8).
evidence: This is based on cell type enrichment analysis using a publicly available database, with results shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2–8.

claim: Resilient non aggressive females (SNagg) showed more DEGs (Hypo-363; PFC-2475) than SEagg males.
source: Resilient non aggressive females (SNagg) showed more DEGs (Hypo-363; PFC-2475) than SEagg males when compared to their respective control samples (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a comparison of transcriptome analysis results between males and females presented in Figure 2.

claim: In Hypo, 16 DEGs overlapped between male and female, with 15 showing expression changes in opposite direction and 1 in similar direction.
source: In Hypo, 16 DEGs overlapped between male and female, 15 showing expression changes in opposite direction, 1 in similar direction and 33 genes were exclusive to SEagg males (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a comparison of transcriptome data between sexes presented in Figure 2D.

claim: 33 genes were exclusive to SEagg males in hypothalamus.
source: In Hypo, 16 DEGs overlapped between male and female, 15 showing expression changes in opposite direction, 1 in similar direction and 33 genes were exclusive to SEagg males (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a comparison of transcriptome data between sexes presented in Figure 2D.

claim: In PFC, 44 DEGs overlapped between male and female, with 29 genes showing expression changes in opposite direction and 15 genes in similar direction.
source: In PFC, 44 DEGs overlapped between male and female, 29 genes showing expression changes in opposite direction and 15 genes in similar direction.
evidence: This is a comparison of transcriptome data between sexes.

claim: Ttr was the topmost ranking gene in Hypo of the transcriptome data in males.
source: Ttr, encoding for thyroid hormone (TH) transporter protein was the topmost ranking gene in Hypo of our transcriptome data in males (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ttr was the only gene showing unique brain region and sex specific diametrically opposite pattern.
source: Further, it was the only gene showing unique brain region and sex specific diametrically opposite pattern (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TH signaling was one of the top ranking pathways in gene ontology enrichment analysis using KEGG tool.
source: Gene ontology enrichment analysis using KEGG tool combined with literature mining also showed TH signaling as one of the top ranking pathways (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Nrgn and Trh were amongst the top ranking genes in Hypo.
source: TH signaling genes Nrgn and Trh was amongst the top ranking genes in Hypo (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In PPS-induced SEagg males, Ttr mRNA showed a decrease of 0.23-fold in Hypo and a robust increase of 8-fold in PFC relative to control males.
source: In PPS-induced SEagg males, Ttr mRNA showed a decrease of 0.23-fold in Hypo and a robust increase of 8-fold in PFC relative to control (Ctrl) males.
evidence: This is RT-PCR validation data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: In adult females that did not show aggressive behavior (SNAgg), Ttr mRNA expression pattern was opposite to males, being increased in Hypo (13.6-fold) and drastically reduced (0.55-fold) in PFC relative to control counterparts.
source: On the contrary, adult females that did not show aggressive behavior (SNAgg), Ttr mRNA expression pattern was opposite to males, being increased in Hypo (13.6-fold) and drastically reduced (0.55-fold) in PFC relative to control counterparts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is RT-PCR validation data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Three-way ANOVA showed a significant effect for brain region x sex x treatment interaction for Ttr mRNA expression in adult mice.
source: Three-way ANOVA showed a significant effect for brain region x sex x treatment interaction {F (1, 88)=685.0, p<0.0001}, significant main effect for treatment {F (1, 88)=98.53, p<0.0001}, sex {F (1, 88)=640.3, p<0.0001} and for brain region (F (1, 88)=1913, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is statistical analysis of Ttr mRNA expression data shown in Figure 3B and detailed in Table 1.

claim: PPS caused drastic reduction in Hypo (0.40-fold) and increase in PFC of Ttr mRNA expression (22.3-fold) of males at peripuberty.
source: PPS caused drastic reduction in Hypo (0.40-fold) and increase in PFC of Ttr mRNA expression (22.3-fold) of males.
evidence: This is RT-PCR data from peripubertal mice presented in Figure 3C.

claim: In females at peripuberty, Ttr mRNA changes were reverse being upregulated (13.12-fold) in Hypo and reduced (0.51-fold) in PFC of PPS mice relative to unstressed controls.
source: In females, the changes were reverse being upregulated (13.12-fold) in Hypo and reduced (0.51-fold) in PFC of PPS mice relative to unstressed (NS) controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is RT-PCR data from peripubertal mice presented in Figure 3C.

claim: TTR protein was reduced to 0.37-fold in Hypo and upregulated by 1.36-fold in PFC in PPS-induced SEagg males, relative to control animals.
source: TTR protein was reduced to 0.37-fold in Hypo and upregulated by 1.36-fold in PFC in PPS-induced SEagg males, relative to control (Ctrl) animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is immunoblot analysis data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant main effect of treatment and brain region as well as interaction for TTR protein levels.
source: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant main effect of treatment {F (1, 8)=10.17, p=0.0128} and brain region {F (1, 8)=60.87, p<0.0001} as well as interaction {F (1, 8)=90.32, p<0.0001}
evidence: This is statistical analysis of TTR protein data shown in Figure 3D and detailed in Table 3.

claim: TTR immunoreactive cells were observed in dorsomedial hypothalamus, ventromedial hypothalamus and arcuate nucleus.
source: TTR immunoreactive cells were observed in dorsomedial hypothalamus, ventromedial hypothalamus and arcuate nucleus.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: Dorsomedial hypothalamus showed more TTR immunoreactive cells than the other sub-regions.
source: Dorsomedial hypothalamus showed more TTR immunoreactive cells than the other sub-regions.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: In SEagg males, TTR protein fluorescence intensity was significantly reduced in Hypo and increased in PFC as compared to Ctrl males.
source: In SEagg males, TTR protein fluorescence intensity was significantly reduced in Hypo (Figure 3E) and increased in PFC as compared to Ctrl males. (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: TTR protein fluorescence intensity in choroid plexus region did not show any difference between Ctrl and SEagg group.
source: Next we investigated TTR protein fluorescence intensity in choroid plexus region, considered to be the main site of TTR protein synthesis in brain, though it did not show any difference between Ctrl and SEagg group. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Circulating TH including total T4 and T3 in serum was neither altered in adulthood nor at peripubertal age in both sexes.
source: Circulating TH including total T4 and T3 in serum (Figure 4B-E and Figure 4—source data 1) was neither altered in adulthood nor at peripubertal age in both sexes.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of serum T4 and T3 shown in Figures 4B-E.

claim: In adult SEagg males, total T4 and T3 was reduced in Hypo but increased in PFC as compared to control samples.
source: In adult SEagg males, total T4 and T3 was reduced in Hypo but increased in PFC as compared to control samples (Ctrl) (Figure 4F and G and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of brain T4 and T3 shown in Figures 4F and G.

claim: Two way ANOVA analyses revealed significant interaction between brain region and treatment for T4 content in adult males.
source: Two way ANOVA analyses revealed significant interaction between brain region and treatment {F (1, 16)=408.3, p<0.0001} as well as main effect of treatment {F (1, 16)=6.711, p=0.0197} though significant main effect of brain region was not observed for changes in T4 content.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of T4 content data shown in Figure 4F and detailed in Table 4.

claim: Two-way ANOVA analyses of T3 content in brain revealed significant main effect of brain region, treatment and interaction in adult males.
source: Two-way ANOVA analyses of T3 content in brain revealed significant main effect of brain region {F (1, 16)=426.7, p<0.0001}, treatment {F (1, 16)=100.2, p<0.0001} and interaction {F (1, 16)=200.5, p<0.0001}.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of T3 content data shown in Figure 4G and detailed in Table 5.

claim: Changes of hypothalamic and PFC T4 and T3 content were persistent from early peripubertal age in males.
source: These changes of hypothalamic and PFC T4 and T3 content was persistent from early peripubertal (NS vs PPS males) age (Figure 4H and I and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of brain T4 and T3 at peripubertal age shown in Figures 4H and I.

claim: In females, direction of changes for both T4 and T3 levels were reverse being increased in Hypo and reduced in PFC but remained unaffected in serum.
source: In females, direction of changes for both T4 and T3 levels were reverse being increased in Hypo and reduced in PFC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1) but remained unaffected in serum.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TH responsive Nrgn mRNA expression showed significant downregulation of 0.5-fold in SEagg males compared to Ctrl males in Hypo.
source: TH responsive Nrgn mRNA expression showed significant downregulation of 0.5-fold in SEagg males compared to Ctrl males (Figure 4K) in Hypo similar to Ttr mRNA.
evidence: This is RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: NRGN protein level was reduced to 0.6-fold in hypothalamus of Eagg males.
source: NRGN protein level was also reduced to 0.6-fold in hypothalamus of Eagg males (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is immunoblot data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Trh showed a robust increase of 5-fold in Hypo of SEagg males while remained unaltered in PFC.
source: Another, TH regulated gene, Trh showed a robust increase of 5-fold in Hypo of SEagg males while remained unaltered in PFC (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Hypothalamus targeted Ttr knockdown to 0.2-fold (80% reduction) in adult unstressed males mirrored the escalated aggression induced by PPS.
source: Hypothalamus targeted Ttr knockdown to 0.2-fold (80% reduction) in adult unstressed males mirrored the escalated aggression induced by PPS (Video 1- Scrambled injected mouse and Video 2 Ttr siRNA injected mouse).
evidence: This is based on stereotaxic injection experiments with behavioral and molecular analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Escalated aggression in Ttr esiRNA injected male mice was prominent as they showed very short average attack latency of ~15 seconds and spent 60.5% of total behavioral RI session in clinch attack.
source: Escalated aggression in these Ttr esiRNA injected male mice was prominent as they showed very short average attack latency of ~15 seconds and spent 60.5% of total behavioral RI session in clinch attack while none of the scrambled control animals showed signs of attack (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is behavioral data from Ttr knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: T3 content in hypothalamus was decreased from 0.07 ng/mg tissue wt in scramble treated group to 0.03 ng/mg tissue wt in Ttr esiRNA treated group.
source: T3 content in hypothalamus was decreased from 0.07 ng/mg tissue wt in scramble treated group to 0.03 ng/mg tissue wt in Ttr esiRNA treated group (Figure 5C and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is ELISA data from Ttr knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TH-responsive Trh mRNA was markedly increased by 6.5-fold upon Ttr gene silencing.
source: TH-responsive Trh mRNA was also markedly increased by 6.5-fold and Nrgn mRNA got reduced to 0.36-fold upon Ttr gene silencing.
evidence: This is RT-PCR data from Ttr knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Nrgn mRNA was reduced to 0.36-fold upon Ttr gene silencing.
source: TH-responsive Trh mRNA was also markedly increased by 6.5-fold and Nrgn mRNA got reduced to 0.36-fold upon Ttr gene silencing.
evidence: This is RT-PCR data from Ttr knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Hairless (Hr) showed maximal downregulation to 0.2-fold upon Ttr gene silencing in hypothalamus.
source: Here, we included another well-established TH responsive gene hairless (Hr) that showed maximal downregulation to 0.2-fold upon Ttr gene silencing in hypothalamus (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is RT-PCR data from Ttr knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Chemically induced increase in T4 levels by injecting levothyroxine in PFC did not show any significant behavioral changes.
source: Chemically induced increase in T4 levels by injecting levothyroxine in PFC did not show any significant behavioral changes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from levothyroxine injection experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: F1 male progenies of SEagg-F0 males showed similar escalated aggressive behavior that characterized the parental generation.
source: F1 male progenies of SEagg-F0 males showed similar escalated aggressive behavior that characterized the parental generation including short attack latency, attack towards anesthetized and female intruder and now referred to as Eagg-F1.
evidence: This is behavioral data from F1 generation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Eagg-F1 male progenies spent 45% of RI observation time in clinch attack with extremely short attack latency of 11 s while males from control F0 did not exhibit attack.
source: These Eagg-F1 male progenies spent 45% of RI observation time in clinch attack with extremely short attack latency of 11 s while males from control F0 did not exhibit attack (Figure 6B and C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is behavioral data from F1 generation shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Female siblings of SEagg-F0 males did not display any prominent sign of aggression.
source: However, female siblings of SEagg-F0 males did not display any prominent sign of aggression.
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral testing of F1 females.

claim: Similar to SEagg-F0 father, Eagg-F1 males showed deficiency in hypothalamic T3 content while that of PFC was not altered.
source: Similar to SEagg-F0 father, Eagg-F1 males showed deficiency in hypothalamic T3 content while that of PFC was not altered (Figure 6D and Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is ELISA data from F1 generation shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Ttr expression reduced to 0.35-fold in the Hypo of Eagg-F1 males without any significant change in the PFC.
source: Ttr expression reduced to 0.35-fold in the Hypo of Eagg-F1 males without any significant change in the PFC.
evidence: This is RT-PCR data from F1 generation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Nrgn showed reduction to 0.35-fold in hypothalamus of Eagg-F1 males.
source: Nrgn (reduction to 0.35-fold) and Trh (upregulation by 4.3-fold) were also altered similarly in hypothalamus (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is RT-PCR data from F1 generation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Trh showed upregulation by 4.3-fold in hypothalamus of Eagg-F1 males.
source: Nrgn (reduction to 0.35-fold) and Trh (upregulation by 4.3-fold) were also altered similarly in hypothalamus (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is RT-PCR data from F1 generation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: MedIP qPCR showed that PPS trigger changes in Ttr DNA methylation in Hypo and PFC in adulthood.
source: As anticipated, MedIP qPCR showed that PPS trigger changes in Ttr DNA methylation in Hypo and PFC in adulthood.
evidence: This is based on MeDIP-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: 5-methylcytosine fold enrichment analyses showed increase in Hypo (9.79-fold) and reduction (0.28-fold) in PFC in SEagg males relative to control.
source: 5-methylcytosine fold enrichment analyses showed increase in Hypo (9.79-fold) and reduction (0.28-fold) in PFC in SEagg males relative to control (Ctrl) (Figure 7 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is MeDIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7.

claim: TTR is a 55 kDa protein that is synthesized in choroid plexus epithelial cells of the brain.
source: TTR is a 55 kDa protein that is synthesized in choroid plexus epithelial cells of the brain (Alshehri et al., 2015)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Alshehri et al., 2015.

claim: TTR was identified in neurons and astrocytes indicating wide expression of the protein in CNS.
source: until recently it was identified in neurons (Li et al., 2011; Zawiślak et al., 2017) and astrocytes indicating wide expression of the protein in CNS.
evidence: This is based on citations to Li et al., 2011 and Zawiślak et al., 2017.

claim: TTR expression in PFC was similar to brain endothelial cell marker proteins.
source: TTR expression in PFC was similar to brain endothelial cell marker proteins (Tang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison with data from Tang et al., 2017.

claim: Cell type specificity analysis using publicly available databases revealed highest expression Ttr mRNA in endothelial cells followed by neurons, microglia and astrocytes in mouse brain.
source: Our cell type specificity analysis using publicly available databases also revealed highest expression Ttr mRNA in endothelial cells followed by neurons, microglia and astrocytes in mouse brain.
evidence: This is based on analysis using the Barres Lab database (https://www.brainrnaseq.org/).

claim: TTR is involved in the uptake of T4 from blood to CSF and local distribution of TH in brain.
source: TTR is involved in the uptake of T4 from blood to CSF and local distribution of TH in brain (Alshehri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Alshehri et al., 2015.

claim: TTR has been assigned other functions including proteolysis of Neuropeptide Y, neuroprotection and regeneration of damaged neurons.
source: TTR has also been assigned other functions including proteolysis of Neuropeptide Y (Nunes et al., 2006), neuroprotection and regeneration of damaged neurons (Sousa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on citations to Nunes et al., 2006 and Sousa et al., 2004.

claim: TH action in developing brain have been considered as critical determinants of multiple neurological deficits.
source: Also, TH action in developing brain have been considered as critical determinants of multiple neurological deficits (Préau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to Préau et al., 2015.

claim: Nrgn is a brain specific TH responsive gene that contains TRE elements in promoter and its transcription is dependent on TH in brain.
source: Nrgn is one such brain specific TH responsive gene that was also amongst the top ranking DEGs in our transcriptome data containing TRE elements in promoter and its transcription is dependent on TH in brain (Pak et al., 2000; Husson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on citations to Pak et al., 2000 and Husson et al., 2004.

claim: Nrgn regulates synaptic plasticity by activating calmodulin kinase II (CaMKII) protein and spine density.
source: Nrgn regulates synaptic plasticity by activating calmodulin kinase II (CaMKII) protein and spine density.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nrgn function.

claim: Previous studies suggest that TH changes in neonatal brain can elicit neuroendocrine abnormalities in their F1 progenies.
source: Previous studies suggest that TH changes in neonatal brain can elicit neuroendocrine abnormalities in their F1 progenies.
evidence: This is a general statement about previous research findings.

claim: Developmental exposure of thyroxine disrupting chemicals can affect gene expression and behavior in later generations.
